articles.title: Poppi founder Allison Ellsworth just launched a new beverage brand — here’s the 411 on Jetty
articles.summary: Poppi founder Allison Ellsworth just launched Jetty, a hydration brand that sells drinks and powders. She gave NBC Selected a behind-the-scenes look into building it.
articles.body: Poppi co-founder Allison Ellsworth knows what you’re thinking: Why would she start another beverage brand after a wildly successful $1.95 billion exit last year? She jokes that she could have retired, but she saw a need her expertise could fill, and she wanted to disrupt the hydration market the same way Poppi redefined how people think of soda. Meet Jetty, which makes its official debut today on its website, Amazon and Target, as well as in Whole Foods stores nationwide. It sells ready-to-drink bottles and ready-to-mix electrolyte powders, but it’s not a sports drink, and it’s not that sodium-heavy stuff made for athletes. “When we started looking at it, we realized that hydration products are made for extremes. They’re for sports and they’re so intense — there was nothing for just simply living,” says Ellsworth, who is the brand’s co-founder and chief brand officer alongside Stephen Ellsworth, her husband, as co-founder and CEO. “We formulated Jetty as close to coconut water — nature’s hydration — as possible without that crazy coconut water taste.” Right before it launched, I talked to Ellsworth about building Jetty, and the lessons she learned during her time at Poppi that she’s applying to running her new company. I also asked her about the products that keep her going throughout her very busy days. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Jetty’s drinks and powders come in five flavors, and Ellsworth’s current favorite is orange mango. “We never had a mango flavor at Poppi, so it was one of the first flavors we formulated for Jetty,” she says. “Orange-flavored products can get really Emergen-C tasting — that’s exactly what I didn’t want. I wanted something fresh, tropical, chuggable and refreshing, which is what it is.” While Ellsworth is excited for customers to finally drink Jetty, she’s equally looking forward to interacting with them online. She took big swings with Poppi to create engaging social media moments that made customers want to buy the products. She also never shied away from making Poppi a founder-led brand. You’ve probably seen her go viral on social media: To date, she has hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram. With Jetty, Ellsworth is following a similar playbook, but she started amassing a loyal customer base before anyone got to try the drinks and powders. Prior to launch, customers began following the brand’s social media accounts and signing up for its SMS and email lists for a chance to win a J-Card, a.k.a. an American Express Black Card, but for Jetty. “We had this really unique opportunity to market a product before its launch, and build hype behind it that you can only capture once,” says Ellswoth. “We saw all this data about how people want physical things, which led to the J-Card. It’s an actual card that we’re giving away a limited amount of per year, and people already signed up to get one. It will give them access to stuff nobody else has, like early access to product drops, pop ups, deals and swag. We’re looking at it as a way to build ride-or-die customers from the beginning because at the end of the day, they’re your community.” To enter to win a J-Card, sign up for Jetty’s email and SMS list — the brand is randomly picking people on a rolling basis. As a now two-time founder launching and promoting a brand-new business while raising three young sons, Ellsworth relies on a few key products to keep her going. “I’m very into beauty and longevity, especially with how much I’m traveling,” she says. “The TheraFace is such a hack, and I love when it gets cold for my under eyes. If I’m traveling and I’m up late, it’s the only thing that makes me look and feel better. A lot of times you have to freeze facial rollers before using them, but when I’m traveling, I obviously don’t have a freezer with me, so the TheraFace is so much easier and works better.” “Yise from Molly Sims has these pads for your face that have transformed my skin,” says Ellsworth. “They’ve gotten rid of my acne and dark spots, and brightened my skin. I just started using them in the last two months, and I absolutely won’t leave the house without them now.” “I always need to have a good lip,” says Ellsworth. “I can have no makeup on, but I need to put on my Rhode Peptide Lip, and I have a Laura Mercier lip gloss that I love, too.” “The one thing that I’m probably the most obsessed with is my Orion sleep system,” says Ellsworth. “It’s basically like an Oura Ring for your body. It’s a pad that goes on top of your mattress, and the temperature changes with your sleep cycle, so if you start to heat up, it cools down. It helps keep you in REM sleep longer, and then it measures your sleep score. When I’m traveling and I don’t have it, I’ll wake up in the middle of the night sweating and I’m like, I miss my Orion.” Ellsworth’s favorite snack when she’s on the go? “I love Solely’s fruit jerky, because not only can I eat it, but my kids can eat it, too,” she says. “It’s real — you don’t feel like you’re eating gummies full of red dye 40.” Ellsworth also reaches for Chomps to get some protein in, but there’s one thing she craves most of all. “For better or for worse, my favorite food in the entire world is a good salt and vinegar chip, like a Miss Vickie’s, and string cheese,” she says. “You’ve got your beef stick, cheese, fruit jerky and chips — that’s all your nutrients right there. It’s my girl dinner.” Why trust NBC Selected? articles.title: What ‘catastrophic’ South Africa local election results mean for ANC
articles.summary: The country is transitioning away from the era of ANC electoral dominance towards a more fragmented political system.
articles.body:
South Africa’s African National Congress (ANC) has recorded its worst-ever result in local elections , more than three decades after the party of Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democratic rule.

While the ANC remains the country’s largest party, Wednesday’s vote appeared to confirm it is locked in a downward spiral amid long-held anger over corruption scandals and poor service delivery.

The elections were held to choose local government councillors who run South Africa’s eight biggest cities as well as its 44 district and 205 local municipalities. ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula described the results of the vote as “catastrophic”.

President Cyril Ramaphosa, who also serves as the president of the ANC, said political parties should approach upcoming political negotiations to form coalitions for local rule with humility. “Our people’s interest must not be drowned by the ⁠quest of political parties or representatives to settle political scores or petty squabbles,” he said.

The ANC won 31 percent of the vote, versus about 25 percent for its main rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA).

The DA has sought to shed its historical reputation as a “white party”, a label it rejects. The party said it had won the votes of more than one million Black South ⁠Africans for the first time, based on its modelling.

The ANC lost its place as the largest party to the DA in the economic hub of Johannesburg, the capital Pretoria, and the large Ekurhuleni municipality east of Johannesburg. The DA also retained its control of South Africa’s second-biggest city, Cape Town.

While the ANC remained the largest party in terms of vote share, the results represent a sharp drop from the 46 percent it bagged in the 2021 local vote and less than half the vote share that the party had two decades ago: 66 percent in 2006.

In 2024, it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time in a national election, which brought about a coalition national government and a seismic shift in South African politics with the end of the ANC’s 30-year dominance.

South Africa held its first democratic elections in 1994, when the ANC won 63 percent of the vote under Mandela’s leadership. He was inaugurated as the first Black president of South Africa shortly afterwards.

Sandile Mnguni, a lecturer in political science and international relations at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, said the “decline in electoral support should serve as a clear warning that the party can no longer rely on its historical political dominance or liberation credentials to retain the confidence of voters”.

“If the underlying grievances of the electorate remain unaddressed, the party could face even greater electoral challenges,” he told Al Jazeera.

Since no party won more than 50 percent of the vote in many cities, the ANC and DA have to team up or hash it out with smaller parties to form municipal governments. Parties have 14 days to negotiate before city councils are formed.

An ANC partnership with the DA would mirror an arrangement they have had in national government for the past two years, but the two are ideologically opposed on key issues ⁠such as how to address the deep economic and social inequalities left by apartheid.

The DA will be mindful of striking a partnership with the ANC, which analysts say was harshly rebuked by voters in this election over problems with basic services such as irregular water, electricity outages, dilapidated roads, broken street lights, and uncollected refuse.

Ramaphosa was also punished for being implicated in a corruption scandal known as “Farmgate” after burglars broke into his luxury private ranch in 2020 and stole $580,000 hidden inside furniture. The president was accused of covering up the theft and keeping efforts to trace the burglars private in a bid to avoid an investigation into where the money had come from.

South African author and political commentator Ralph Mathekga told Al Jazeera that the vote sent a “strong message” to the ANC “that the collapse of service delivery and the ensuing corruption has reached a point where it cannot be tolerated”.

Mathekga said voters no longer see the party as the solution to the problems faced by South Africans, but as the “chief culprit”.

“The elections were clearly a referendum on the ANC ‘s capacity to govern and turn the corner,” he noted.

South African political analyst and columnist Sipho Seepe said the vote was also a personal rebuke of Ramaphosa, who sought to present himself as a politically savvy and business-oriented leader for the party, but who has continually been accused of underperforming.

“He has been a total disaster, and the people this time have made it very clear,” Seepe told Al Jazeera. “People have been giving it [the ANC] a chance, and [now] they’re saying no more.”

The DA suggested it would steer clear of an agreement with the ANC when it said in a statement that it would initiate coalition discussions with “political parties that share a commitment to clean and accountable government, rooting out corruption, service delivery for all, the rule of law, and non-racialism”.

Ramaphosa is expected to step aside as party leader ahead of the 2027 ANC leadership contest and the country’s next general election in 2029.

What does this vote mean for South Africa?

The local election has ramifications for South Africa’s politics beyond local government.

Analysts say the vote confirms that the country is transitioning away from one-party dominance and towards political plurality. “From now on, we can accept coalitions to be the new normal,” Seepe said.

While this might lead to some political instability, the analyst said it may pressure parties to prioritise performance once in power. “The ANC government has been stable, but it has been failing the people,” he said, noting that being responsive to the electorate’s needs is now seen as more urgent than political continuity.

Mathekga, author of the book The ANC’s Last Decade, said voters have made it clear that they “do not want concentration of power in one party”.

“Coalitions are there to stay, perhaps until political parties demonstrate that they can be trusted with power to constitute government on their own,” Mathekga said, describing the shift as a “necessary evolution of South African politics”.

Mnguni, at the University of KwaZulu-Natal, agreed that South Africa appeared to be ready to trade a little less political stability in exchange for greater accountability.

“Of course, there may be instances of political stalemating, unstable alliances and disagreements that delay important municipal decisions [and] these risks should not be underestimated,” he said.

“However, I view the broader transition as an opportunity for South Africa’s democratic development, provided that political parties demonstrate political maturity and place governance above narrow partisan interests.”

articles.title: AI's growing energy appetite revives market for ageing turbines, jet engines
articles.summary: The race to dominate artificial intelligence is creating an unusual scramble in the energy market, with technology companies hunting for equipment that
articles.body: The race to dominate artificial intelligence is creating an unusual scramble in the energy market, with technology companies hunting for equipment that was never originally meant to power data centres.From second-hand gas turbines to retired aircraft jet engines, companies are exploring unconventional ways to secure electricity as the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure runs into a growing shortage of power-generation equipment.According to Reuters, the rush for turbines has intensified as manufacturers struggle to meet demand and delivery timelines for new equipment stretch to as long as six years. With AI data centres demanding enormous amounts of electricity, companies are increasingly looking towards the used equipment market to keep their expansion plans on track.Why are AI companies turning to gas turbines?The growing demand for artificial intelligence is creating an enormous appetite for electricity, with data centres requiring a continuous and reliable power supply to run thousands of high-performance processors.Unlike conventional office buildings, these facilities operate energy-intensive computing systems around the clock, while their cooling infrastructure adds significantly to their overall electricity consumption.As technology companies race to expand their AI infrastructure, securing enough electricity has become a major challenge. Waiting for new grid connections and conventional power infrastructure can delay projects, pushing developers to explore on-site electricity generation. Gas turbines offer a way to generate large amounts of power directly at or near data centre facilities, reducing dependence on external electricity networks.This growing demand is now putting pressure on turbine manufacturers, forcing companies to look beyond newly manufactured equipment and explore the second-hand market.The growing demand is benefiting some of the world's biggest turbine manufacturers, including Siemens Energy, GE Vernova and Japan's Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. These companies are facing a surge in orders as data centre developers and utilities compete for equipment, while their manufacturing capacity struggles to keep pace with demand.The surge in demand is exposing a widening gap between the global supply of gas turbines and the requirements of the power industry. According to Reuters, citing estimates from Wood Mackenzie, global turbine orders have crossed 100 gigawatts (GW), while annual manufacturing capacity stands at just 60-70 GW. The gap is expected to widen further as demand from AI data centres and conventional power projects continues to grow.The pressure is also reflected in delivery timelines. In the United States, companies seeking new gas turbines are facing waiting periods of up to six years. Estimates cited by Reuters suggest that global turbine demand could reach 129 GW in 2028, while manufacturing capacity is expected to rise to only 87 GW.This imbalance is pushing data centre developers towards used and refurbished equipment as they seek alternatives to lengthy waits for newly manufactured turbines.Why used turbines are becoming increasingly valuableWith new gas turbines becoming harder to secure, the second-hand market is emerging as an increasingly attractive option for data centre developers and power companies. Used turbines are reportedly selling for $1.5 million to $1.7 million per megawatt (MW), compared with $2 million to $2.5 million per MW for new equipment. Refurbished units are available for around $1.3 million per MW.The price difference is not the only attraction. Buying pre-owned equipment can also help companies avoid years of waiting for new turbines to arrive. Reuters reported that two 14.5 MW turbines were recently sold for $12.5 million, while comparable new equipment could cost around $35 million and take up to five years to be delivered.The growing competition for second-hand equipment is also creating a new business opportunity for companies that specialise in sourcing, repairing and reselling older power-generation machinery.You use AI every day. articles.title: More than 100,000 sign petition for inquiry into UK role in Gaza genocide
articles.summary: The number of signatures requires the British parliament to consider the topic for debate.
articles.body:
A petition calling for a public inquiry into Britain’s “complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza” has gathered more than 100,000 signatures.

The petition posted on the UK Parliament website reached the threshold on Monday, requiring parliament to consider the topic for debate.

The initiative demands “an inquiry into any British involvement in Israeli operations in Gaza,” including “the sale, supply or use of weapons, surveillance aircraft and Royal Air Force bases”.

The petition was launched by Jennifer Forbes, chair of the executive committee of Your Party, a left-wing party launched by former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn – who serves as its parliamentary leader – and other left-wing figures in the UK.

Signatories called for an inquiry that has the power to question government ministers and officials involved in decision-making around the UK’s role in the war, particularly regarding the supply of arms to Israel.

“We are not going away until we get this inquiry. We want the truth, and we want justice,” Jeremy Corbyn said in a post on X.

The UK is a longstanding ally of Israel and has reportedly supported the country’s genocidal war on Gaza.

A 2024 investigation by Al Jazeera revealed that the UK provided military support to Israel by creating an air bridge that was vital to sustain the intensity of the war on Gaza. Furthermore, UK-based companies and factories supply crucial parts found in jets that are used to bomb Gaza.

However, experts say the UK’s policy towards supporting Israel has shifted in recent months . After assuming leadership in July, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the ruling Labour Party “got wrong” its position on Israel, and accepted that it caused “huge hurt”.

It is not unusual for parliamentary petitions to reach 100,000 signatures in the UK. Examples of petitions active right now with more than 100,000 signatures include one on reducing the pension age and another that demands a stop to the addition of folic acid to flour.

The petitions do not require lawmakers to do anything more than consider the topic for a debate.

articles.title: In 1905, New Jersey received mosquitofish from North Carolina to fight mosquitoes; the species are now considered harmful to resident aquatic wildlife
articles.summary: Discover the unintended consequences of introducing mosquitofish in New Jersey in 1905 for mosquito control, leading to harmful impacts on local aquatic ecosystems and native species.
articles.body: Anyone who has ever stayed awake listening to a mosquito buzz knows the urge to fight back. New Jersey did just that back in 1905, but in an unusual way. The US Geological Survey's Nonindigenous Aquatic Species database says that a small fish called Gambusia, reportedly from North Carolina, was released into New Jersey waters that year to control mosquitoes. The plan seemed smart, simple, and cheap. But over time, the fish ended up becoming a tricky guest. Now they are seen as a threat to wildlife already living in local waters.Why the tiny fish looked like a big solutionMosquitofish got their name because they feed on mosquito larvae, the wriggling young ones that develop in water. This made them appear as an ideal natural pest controller. The USGS explains that people often stocked them with little care in temperate and tropical regions around the world. It adds that groups like the former US Public Health Service released them in the decades that followed. They considered this fish to be a low-cost solution for malaria. The introduction in New Jersey was part of the earliest introductions in the United States, which took place during the early 1900s. In the same year, about 150 fish from Texas were also released in Hawaii. The goal there was to test how well they eat mosquito larvae.Did the fish really work?The USGS notes that critical reviews of research from around the world don't support the view that mosquitofish are especially good at cutting mosquito numbers or mosquito-borne diseases. Neither are they gentle neighbours. The database describes them as aggressive fish that frequently attack other species. They tear off fins and often kill other fish. They eat the eggs, larvae, and young of other fish and also prey on smaller species of adult fish. In some waters, they can even backfire. If they eat the small animals that usually prey on mosquito larvae, instead of falling, mosquito numbers may rise.What this means for local wildlifeNow, New Jersey Fish and Wildlife has adopted a clear view. Its freshwater fish guide classifies the western mosquitofish as non-native, explaining that the fish was cultivated and stocked for mosquito control purposes. The species is considered harmful to populations of resident fish and amphibians. The fish should not be stocked in areas where they may affect native species. However, there is some inconsistency here. In the same guide, eastern mosquitofish is classified as native to the southernmost parts of the state. Moreover, it says that the two species may be difficult to tell apart. According to USGS, many of the early releases were poorly documented, so it is often uncertain what species was moved. One of the strongest pieces of evidence of harm comes from the American West. There, the agency says, the mosquitofish contributed to the decline or local loss of threatened or endangered species. In Arizona, introduced fish, including mosquitofish, are believed to play a part in the decline of the Chiricahua leopard frog.A lesson that still mattersThe 1905 release shows how a quick fix can end up casting a very long shadow. The fish didn't solve the mosquito problem. Instead, they also brought fresh worries for the creatures already living in the water. So, if you ever think of stocking a pond with fish to control mosquitoes, it might be a good idea to consult with local wildlife officials first. A small fish with a good reputation can still do big damage once they settle into a new home.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Civil servant who secretly held five jobs found guilty of fraud
articles.summary: Kashim Chowdhury had secretly held multiple public sector jobs on full-time salaries.
articles.body:
A civil servant who secretly held multiple public sector jobs on full-time salaries has been found guilty of nine counts of fraud.

Kashim Chowdhury, from east London, had five government jobs that overlapped in the spring of 2023. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.

The prosecution accused the 56-year-old of ''deliberate, intentional dishonesty'' and of ''exploiting the system''.

After seven hours of deliberation, the jury unanimously found Chowdhury guilty of eight counts of fraud by false representation and one count of fraud by a failure to disclose.

The judge said Chowdhury faced a ''very significant custodial sentence''. He added he was refusing bail because of the significance of the crime and for Chowdhury's own wellbeing.

"This was sustained and deliberate dishonesty," said Sarah Melo, specialist prosecutor at the CPS Serious Economic Organised Crime and International Directorate.

"He knew he could not legitimately hold multiple full-time positions at the same time, but continued to conceal what he was doing."

A Defra spokesperson said Chowdury "abused the trust placed in him as a public servant", adding that it would use all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending.

Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight full-time public sector roles that overlapped and earned him £350,000 in total.

The prosecution told the court that on application forms he provided inaccurate information about his employment status and failed to disclose to government departments that he was already a civil servant. Once he secured the roles he didn't tell his employers he was working elsewhere.

He was allowed to work entirely from home because he told his employers he was caring for his mother, whom he lived with in east London. She had dementia and was diagnosed with terminal cancer in 2023.

How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long

But rather than reduce his workload to look after her, he kept taking on new jobs. In the spring of 2023, when his mother was a few months away from death, he had jobs at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the Department of Health and Social Care, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office.

During this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Chowdhury said he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment in the past. He was made redundant from a job at the Department for Education in 2013 and was given a diagnosis of PTSD.

He said he had not been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".

But the prosecution barrister, Lucy Organ, told the jury: "He's lied to you in evidence, he's lied to you under oath, which demonstrates the level of deceit he has descended to."

A succession of his managers told the court about his poor performance. Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney who managed Chowdhury at Defra.

He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time". McCartney said that during video calls Chowdhury had his camera switched off blaming technical problems. McCartney said this went on for four to five months.

But McCartney said that because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job and remained there for two years.

The prosecution argued that he used sick notes to cope with his impossible schedule. In March 2023, he was on sick leave from four of the organisations he worked for. But he kept working at the Home Office and did not tell them he was ill.

His line manager at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023. By this point he'd been off sick for three months and she wanted to make a plan to get him back to work.

She told the jury that at the start of the call he was coughing a lot and waving tissues up to the camera. She also told the jury that he had been wearing white make-up to try to look ill.

Adams told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."

Chowdhury told the jury this was a smear and that he had not been wearing make-up.

After the call, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it he blamed a technical error.

Adams grew suspicious. ''I believed he was lying,'' she told the jury. She escalated her concerns up the chain at the UKHSA.

But his fraudulent behaviour went on for several more months until he left the civil service in September 2023.

He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of civil service databases such as payroll every two years to look for anomalies.

Chowdhury has also been accused by his siblings of bullying their mother into increasing his share of the family home days before she died.

In a case at the High Court, Chowdhury's two brothers and sister allege that he put "undue influence" on Faijun Nessa to sign documents that meant he would inherit half of her home.

The four-storey, six-bedroom home in east London has been valued at £2.1m.

His siblings say their mother could not have understood what she was signing because she was "desperately unwell". In January 2023 she was given a terminal diagnosis of stage four metastatic colorectal cancer.

The claimants also allege that Mrs Nessa, who was nearly blind and could not speak English, was unaware of what she was signing because the documents were not translated into her native Bengali at the time they were signed.

Kashim Chowdhury denies the claims. That case is ongoing.

articles.title: After falling for his family's Ontario farm, William Shotyk spent 50 years restoring it, planting 25,000 trees; now, 145 bird species and bald eagles live there
articles.summary: Discover how William Shotyk transformed a barren 72-acre Ontario farm into a thriving wildlife sanctuary over 50 years, planting 25,000 trees and attracting 145 bird species, including majestic bald eagles.
articles.body: For most of us, there is probably a place from our childhood that we hope to return to someday. Few of us spend 50 years taking care of it. William Shotyk did exactly that. In October 2025, BarrieToday reported on his talk in Elmvale, Ontario, where the University of Alberta professor explained how he turned a bare 72-acre farm into a wildlife home. It all started when he was a Grade 8 student from Toronto who asked his father to purchase the land.A teenager’s request and a summer of plantingBarrieToday reports that Shotyk’s father purchased the farm as per his wishes. The University of Alberta’s Folio news site dates the purchase to 1972. Shotyk began planting in 1975, when he was still in high school. In that summer, he planted 2,000 trees of white spruce and red oak. “That's really when I fell in love with the farm,” he told the audience. After some time, he returned with 16 friends and planted 5,000 more seedlings at a penny each. The group slept in the old hay barn. His studies and research work kept him away from the farm, taking him to Europe and later Alberta, where he has been a professor since 2011. Before moving to Europe, he entered into an agreement with the natural resources ministry of Ontario under which the ministry would plant almost 14,000 spruce trees on the farm.More than 25,000 trees and a bold carbon claimThe farm now has more than 25,000 trees, from more than 50 species. By 2012, Folio reported, Shotyk had planted more than 25,000 trees with the help of family and friends. Shotyk says trees provide shelter for crops and livestock buildings, conserve moisture, and offer a home for birds that eat insect pests. They also suck carbon dioxide out of the air, he adds. The concentration of carbon dioxide rose from 315 parts per million when he was born in 1958 to 426 at the time of his talk. He believes that planting so many trees has cancelled out his personal carbon footprint for the next 300 years. That figure is his own estimate, so best read as his view rather than a verified fact.Frogs, turtles, and 145 kinds of birdsShotyk teamed up with Ducks Unlimited in 2016 to build a wetland on the farm. In the fall, it was nothing more than just a hole in the ground. However, by the following spring, it was full of water, and frogs showed up almost immediately. Then there were waterfowl, followed by a painted turtle, and eventually snapping turtles. Shotyk explains that he has no clue how the painted turtle discovered the wetland. The farm has hosted 145 different bird species, including bluebirds, meadowlarks, green herons, and trumpeter swans. The ultimate reward, he said, was a pair of bald eagles that showed up first in 2024.Why the bald eagles matter so muchShotyk says the eagles are important because DDT, a man-made insecticide that was once widely used for pest control, nearly wiped them out. In the early 1960s, he said, almost nobody would have seen a bald eagle in Elmvale. A 1982 study in the journal Science showed that the birds struggled, then bounced back. It followed eagles in northwestern Ontario, where the number of young per breeding area dropped from 1.26 in 1966 to 0.46 in 1974, then rose to 1.12 in 1981. The study was done in another part of Ontario and reflects the larger trend, not the Elmvale birds. Shotyk's farm is just one small patch of land, but it shows what decades of steady work can help bring back.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Tyler Robinson judge gives long-awaited trial date ruling in assassination of Charlie Kirk
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson's trial date ruling comes Monday as prosecutors and defense clash over timelines in the Charlie Kirk assassination case.
articles.body: PROVO, Utah — The judge overseeing the case against accused assassin Tyler Robinson announced his ruling Monday after prosecutors and defense attorneys sought dramatically different start times for the trial of a man accused of gunning down Charlie Kirk last year. Robinson, 22, is accused of assassinating the 31-year-old Kirk on Sept. 10, 2025, during a Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University in Orem by shooting him with a .30-06 hunting rifle from a rooftop on the other side of the campus courtyard. Graf said Monday that Robinson's trial will begin on June 21, 2028, and reserved 105 days. Utah County prosecutors asked in court documents and oral arguments for Jan. 31, 2028, as their preferred trial date but said they could be ready in October 2027. Robinson's defense team has proposed late 2029 as a "soft target" trial date. TYLER ROBINSON HEARING ENDS WITHOUT TRIAL DATE SET, PROMPTING FIERY PLEA FROM ERIKA KIRK'S LAWYER Staci Visser, one of Robinson's defense lawyers, said at a hearing in October that the state's timeline is "not practical" due to large amounts of discovery. "Discovery review is foundational," she said. "It impacts everything else." MICHAEL RUIZ: TYLER ROBINSON BLAMES TRUMP POST IN PUSH FOR CAMERA BAN The court is also attempting to work with both sides to avoid setting a date that conflicts with previously scheduled trials they have in other cases. One directly conflicted with the prosecution's desired start date, a federal racketeering case defense attorney Richard Novak has scheduled for Jan. 10, 2028. "The reality is rushing to trial does not lead to closure. It does not lead to finality. It leads to mistakes," he said at a hearing on Oct. 23. CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION SUSPECT'S LAWYERS MIRROR NOTORIOUS KILLER'S TACTICAL DELAY STRATEGY: FMR PROSECUTOR Both sides agreed that setting a trial earlier, which would be interrupted for a break during the holidays, could put potential jurors and witnesses in a bind. articles.title: New big rig safety tech could save your life
articles.summary: Daimler Truck's Oregon demos show how a Freightliner Cascadia's automatic emergency braking responds when dummy cars suddenly cross a moving truck's path.
articles.body: Ever find yourself driving next to a massive 18-wheeler and wondering if the driver can actually see your car? It's a reasonable concern. Big rigs have enormous blind spots, and stopping one takes a lot more time and distance than stopping your car. Now, new big rig safety tech from Daimler Truck could help prevent some of the most dangerous crashes on our roads. The company behind Freightliner is upgrading its trucks with technology that can recognize potential collisions and automatically hit the brakes. We're talking about situations where another driver suddenly cuts across a truck's path or a pedestrian gets dangerously close during a turn. And demonstrations at Daimler's Oregon proving grounds offer a revealing look at what happens when this technology faces situations that could turn deadly on public roads. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. 100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS What happens when a car suddenly cuts in front of a big rig? At Daimler Truck's testing facility in Oregon, engineers recreated situations that could easily turn deadly on a public road. They used dummy cars mounted on remote-controlled platforms to simulate vehicles suddenly crossing in front of a moving Freightliner Cascadia. In one demonstration, the truck successfully avoided a collision. In another, it clipped the dummy car after braking. That second test may sound like a failure, but consider what could have happened if the truck had continued at full speed. Slowing down before impact can make an enormous difference when a passenger car comes face-to-face with a fully loaded truck. The demonstrations generally took place at speeds between 40 and 55 mph. Daimler said the truck's trailer carried approximately 30,000 pounds during the tests. That's a lot of weight pushing forward when the brakes suddenly engage. And here's what caught my attention. The technology was designed to recognize these developing dangers and respond even when the driver had little time to react. That's especially important because a few seconds can determine how serious a collision becomes. How big rig safety tech spots trouble before a crash The technology comes from Detroit Assurance, Daimler Truck North America's collection of advanced driver assistance systems. At the center is Active Brake Assist 6, also known as ABA6. It uses five radar sensors and a camera to monitor what's happening around the truck. Together, they provide approximately 270 degrees of coverage, including areas alongside a standard 53-foot trailer. Think of it as another set of electronic eyes helping the driver keep track of nearby traffic. The system can identify certain vehicles that have stopped unexpectedly, including cars sitting at unusual angles after an accident. For example, a truck approaching a crash scene might encounter a disabled vehicle partly blocking the roadway. Active Brake Assist 6 is designed to recognize these situations and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes. The technology can recognize pedestrians and cyclists in certain scenarios, too. That's particularly useful when a large truck travels through busy areas where people may be difficult to see from the cab. And Daimler is now expanding those capabilities to address another dangerous situation. WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WAYMO COMPUTER FAILS? New Freightliner safety systems can brake at intersections Intersections can be especially challenging for truck drivers. They have to maneuver a massive vehicle while watching traffic that may approach from several directions. All it takes is one person making an unexpected move. That's where a new feature called Cross Traffic Assist comes in. The system uses radar to detect vehicles crossing the truck's path at intersections. If it recognizes a potential collision, it can alert the driver with audible and visual warnings. When the danger becomes more serious, it can also apply partial or full braking. Now, think about what that could mean if someone accidentally pulls out in front of an approaching truck. The system may give the driver extra time to respond or help reduce the force of a collision. Another improvement involves Active Side Guard Assist 2. The enhanced system adds protection when the truck makes a left turn across oncoming traffic. With the left turn signal activated, it can recognize certain approaching vehicles and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes. The new left-turn protection builds on existing safety technology that monitors the passenger-side blind spot during right turns. That system can detect pedestrians and cyclists and apply braking when necessary. These improvements are scheduled to become standard on Freightliner Cascadias built beginning in 2027, with production planned for January. Active Brake Assist 6 itself is already standard on the fifth-generation Cascadia. According to Daimler Truck North America, the goal is to give professional drivers additional support when visibility or reaction time becomes limited. What if a truck driver suddenly stops responding? There's another feature that deserves attention because it addresses a frightening possibility. What happens if someone behind the wheel of a big rig suddenly becomes unresponsive? Freightliner's optional Active Lane Assist 2 can help keep the truck centered in its lane and correct unintended drifting. It can also provide steering assistance during certain challenging driving conditions, such as strong crosswinds. But the feature I find particularly interesting is called Attentive Driver Protection. When the lane-keeping system is active, Attentive Driver Protection monitors whether the driver continues responding. If the driver fails to respond to escalating warnings, the technology can slow the truck to a stop while helping keep it centered in its lane. It can also activate the hazard lights to warn surrounding traffic. Consider the potential consequences of a driver becoming unresponsive while operating a massive truck on a busy highway. Having an additional safety system that can help bring the vehicle to a controlled stop could make a significant difference. However, the feature doesn't diagnose medical emergencies or determine why a driver has stopped responding. It reacts to a lack of driver response under specific conditions. And like the other safety systems, it still depends on factors such as road conditions and sensor performance. HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN What this means to you You may never drive a Freightliner, but chances are you share the road with big rigs regularly. And that's why these improvements should interest you. If a truck can recognize a dangerous situation and begin braking before the driver has time to react, the people in nearby vehicles could have a better chance of avoiding serious injuries. Even reducing the speed of an unavoidable collision could make a significant difference. But don't assume every truck you encounter has these features. Many older trucks won't have the newest technology, and even equipped vehicles have limitations. Sensors can struggle in poor weather or when visibility becomes limited. Automatic braking also cannot guarantee that every collision will be avoided. So, continue giving big rigs plenty of room. Avoid lingering beside a truck where the driver might have trouble seeing you. And when passing, make sure there's sufficient space before moving back into its lane. Remember that even the smartest technology cannot change the physics of a massive truck traveling at highway speed. The safest approach is to stay alert and avoid putting yourself in a situation where a truck driver has to make a sudden move. Kurt's key takeaways Here's what I find encouraging about Daimler's latest safety technology. It recognizes something we all know about driving. People make mistakes. Someone misjudges an intersection or pulls out without realizing how quickly a truck is approaching. Those split-second decisions can have terrible consequences, especially when a massive vehicle has little room to stop. The demonstrations in Oregon showed why this technology has potential. In one scenario, the truck avoided a collision. In another, contact still occurred, but the braking reduced the impact. That second result is an important reminder that a safety system can still provide protection even when it cannot prevent every accident. I also think we're seeing an interesting shift in how truck manufacturers approach safety. There's been plenty of attention on trucks that can drive themselves. Yet here we have technology designed to help professional drivers do their jobs more safely. And when you consider how many trucks share our highways, even modest improvements in collision prevention could have an enormous impact. Of course, controlled demonstrations are one thing. Everyday traffic brings unexpected challenges that are much harder to predict. I'll be interested to see how these systems perform as more equipped trucks reach the road. If the technology can prevent serious crashes, that's something we can all appreciate. Would you feel safer knowing an 18-wheeler could automatically brake to avoid hitting your car, or would you still be nervous driving alongside a massive truck that relies on software to react? articles.title: Dirty Sanchez star honours Michael 'Pancho' Locke on Everest
articles.summary: MTV's Matthew Pritchard carried a flag to Everest Base Camp in memory of fellow stuntman 'Pancho'.
articles.body:
A tribute flag to Michael "Pancho" Locke has reached Everest Base Camp after his former Dirty Sanchez co-star Mathew Pritchard dedicated his Himalayan trek to the Welsh TV star and entrepreneur.

Locke's former co-conspirator on the MTV stunt and prank series had already started the challenge when he learned of the news of Locke's death on Friday.

The Cardiff presenter and skateboarder said he was now heading home to "give Panch a send-off", after spending the journey reflecting on more than 35 years of friendship.

"He had the biggest heart and was one of the kindest souls you could ever meet," he said, adding there was "never, ever a dull moment" with Locke.

In a tribute posted during the trek, Pritchard reflected on the pair's decades-long friendship, saying Locke "was the only person I knew who could make you laugh without even trying".

Pritchard also revealed he had recently spent time with Locke at his shop - memories, he said, he would "always treasure".

"It's almost as if the universe gave us that one last bit of time together before taking him away. I'll always treasure that," he wrote.

"I wish I could hear your voice one more time. I miss you, and I'll always love you."

The UK equivalent to US stunt film series Jackass, Dirty Sanchez started out in Newport and saw the group travel all over the world performing stunts and pranks.

Locke, Pritchard, Lee Dainton and Dan Joyce starred in the MTV show, which ran from 2003 to 2007, airing in 64 countries and garnering more than 400 million viewers.

Further tributes have appeared on social media from friends and supporters in Port Talbot where Locke became co-owner of streetwear brand San Portablo in 2016.

Flowers were left outside the shop in the Aberafan shopping centre and San Portablo shared images of a mural created in Locke's memory.

His partner in the business, former Tata steelworker Nigel Hunt, told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast , Locke was someone whose presence was felt wherever he went.

"He had a brilliant life," said Hunt. "He lit up rooms, he lit up the world."

Hunt said Locke was fiercely loyal to his friends and was known for championing local musicians, comedians and artists.

Recalling his support for comedian Sandro Ford, he said Locke would travel to small gigs across the country, simply to make sure there was a friendly face in the audience.

Ford dedicated a show in Neath to Locke over the weekend, receiving a standing ovation when he described him as "a legend" and "a good friend" who had helped him throughout his career.

Hunt said: "He loved seeing people do well. He encouraged people."

Describing Locke as "wild", "messy" and "rock and roll", Hunt said he was also "an extremely loyal friend" whose impact on the creative life of Port Talbot would be felt for years to come.

He predicted an "incredible display of love" for Locke in the coming weeks, with musicians, artists and members of the local community all planning tributes.

Fellow Dirty Sanchez star Dainton said news of Locke's death had brought back memories of the group's early days skateboarding together.

"When you grow up skating with your friends, you're in your own little world. You never think about losing anyone from it," he wrote.

"Since hearing the news, all those memories have been flooding back.

"I can see Panch, hear the laughter and remember all the best times like it was yesterday.

"Then it hits me that he's gone and I still can't believe it," he wrote, adding his thoughts were with Locke's daughters, family and friends.

articles.title: More than 50,000 displaced by deadly Ethiopia border clashes
articles.summary: Families arrive in Kenya with little food or shelter as host communities struggle to cope.
articles.body:
Moyale, Kenya – When Hawa Hassan fled her home in Ethiopia’s Moyale area, she left almost everything behind. Her house was burned during the violence, she said. But one memory has stayed with her: a 13-year-old girl shot while sitting near a wall.

Hassan said the girl had not touched a flag, a detail she raised while describing tensions over flag displays in the disputed border area. Her account of the killing could not be independently verified.

The journey into Kenya was brutal. Hassan told Al Jazeera that some women gave birth while fleeing, and that families arrived without food, cooking utensils or bedding. Newborn babies were sleeping on bare floors. Diarrhoea was spreading, while families feared malaria as mosquitoes multiplied.

For many, crossing the border has meant escaping gunfire only to face another struggle: finding food and shelter. The arrivals are also stretching Kenyan communities. Families that opened their homes are sharing scarce supplies, even as some worry the violence could reach their own neighbourhoods.

A government-led assessment conducted on October 29 and 30 estimated that 35,950 people had been displaced as of October 24. About 25,000 were staying with host families and nearly 11,000 in temporary displacement sites.

The number has since risen. During a meeting, Kenya Red Cross regional head Malik Adan said the number of people displaced by the conflict had increased from an estimated 36,000 to more than 50,000. The figure includes people living in temporary settlements as well as those staying with relatives and host families.

The overall number of displaced people has yet to be independently established, and no final figure has been confirmed.

The assessment covered 758 households and involved government authorities, United Nations agencies, the Kenya Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations. The figures reflect different reporting periods.

The fighting is rooted in a long-standing dispute over land and administrative control between Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations. Tensions escalated around October 18 over the raising of the Somali regional flag in the disputed Moyale area, reflecting competing claims over territory and authority.

For those arriving in Kenya, the politics are secondary to the immediate question of where they will sleep and what they will feed their children.

Mwasaru Mercy, Kenya’s acting commissioner for refugee affairs, told Al Jazeera that a multi-agency government team had been deployed to Moyale. The Department of Refugee Services is coordinating with local authorities and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

But gunfire could still be heard, Mercy said, raising fears of further displacement. Many arrivals need food, shelter, bedding and mosquito nets.

“There are no contingency food stocks specifically for this incident because it happened abruptly,” Mercy said.

Authorities are trying to mobilise humanitarian organisations and donors. A refugee camp has not been established because the security situation must improve first. The government is working with UNHCR to register arrivals and assess their needs.

Those affected include Ethiopians fleeing violence, traders, and Kenyans forced from their homes by stray ammunition, Mercy said.

Fatima Mohammed Cole, UNHCR’s representative in Kenya, said many arrivals were women and children. Families are spread across several locations, including six sites hosting Ethiopians. They need shelter, food and healthcare, while crowded conditions raise concerns about the spread of disease.

Cole said gunfire was still being heard in Moyale and appealed for a ceasefire that would allow families to return home.

The response is also under way inside Ethiopia. The Ethiopian Red Cross Society said it had provided emergency shelter and household items worth about 30 million Ethiopian birr ($182,970) to 1,000 households displaced from Moyale town and surrounding areas.

The supplies included 2,000 tarpaulins, blankets and sleeping mats, as well as dignity kits, jerrycans, kitchen sets, soap and solar lamps. Distribution was under way, the organisation said. The operation is separate from assistance in Kenya.

In Kenya, residents who initially opened their doors are finding it harder to keep going.

Abdi Maalim, a member of the Moyale Cross-Border Peace Committee, told Al Jazeera that some Kenyan families had moved further inland after bullets and heavy weapons landed close to their homes. He called for more border patrols to prevent armed groups from crossing into Kenya.

Families that once cooked for five or six people are now feeding 20 or 30.

Moyale’s role as a trading point between Kenya and Ethiopia has added to the strain. Maalim said trucks carrying goods between Mombasa and Addis Ababa had been stranded near the border for almost two weeks. Kenyan trucks were also stuck in Ethiopia, and businesses in Moyale had slowed sharply.

Bank closures have disrupted the circulation of the Ethiopian birr. Traders reported price rises of about 20 percent as supplies became harder to move.

Security analyst Dr Abdiwahab Sheikh Abdisamad told Al Jazeera that the clashes had grown beyond a local dispute over territory, exposing deeper ethnic divisions and political competition between Ethiopia’s regional administrations.

He said perceptions of Oromo expansionism and allegations of federal government support for Oromia’s regional leadership risked deepening mistrust. He warned that armed fighters crossing the border, stray bullets and further displacement made this a Kenyan security concern as well as a refugee emergency.

Kenya’s Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, said additional officers would be deployed along the border to strengthen security. During a visit to Moyale on November 5, he said Kenya was engaging Ethiopia’s federal government to help end the conflict.

Kanja said about 10,000 people were staying in temporary shelters and public institutions, while others had been taken in by host families. He said one Kenyan had died after being hit by a stray bullet, while a police report indicated that an Ethiopian man had also died from gunshot wounds sustained in Kenya.

The 10,000 figure refers to people in temporary shelters and public institutions, not the total number displaced. It is not directly comparable with the Red Cross estimate of more than 50,000, which includes people staying with host families.

Hassan wants to return home, but only when it is safe. Until then, she and thousands of others depend on host communities and humanitarian agencies. The longer the fighting continues, the harder it will be for those communities to keep absorbing the cost.

Maalim said residents had already stretched their resources to accommodate the new arrivals.

“Previously, we were supplying this town alone. Now we are literally taking care of two towns together,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: France accuses Iran of cyberattack on supermarket fridges
articles.summary: Paris says a cyber unit linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard was behind hack, which hit more than 1,000 stores.
articles.body:
France has opened an investigation and accused Iran of being behind recent cyberattacks targeting refrigeration units in supermarkets.

French authorities said on Monday that they are probing a cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) over the attacks, which caused fires and large amounts of food waste.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said that the Iranian ambassador had been summoned and that sanctions would be brought against Iran at a “European level”.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Barrot said of the cyberattacks on French supermarkets that occurred October 11 and 12.

The Paris prosecutor’s ⁠office said ⁠it has requested international arrest warrants against ⁠the leader ⁠of Shahid Kaveh, ⁠an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Revolutionary ‌Guards, and his two ‌deputies.

Barrot told reporters that the attack was “unprecedented in its level of aggression”.

“This is the first large-scale cyberattack carried out for sabotage purposes on French soil,” he said. “It represents a major attack on the nation’s interests and on the security of the French people. That is why it will not go unanswered.

“We will also take any other measures that are proportionate and necessary, whether public or private, to respond to this attack and deter anyone who might seek to repeat it,” Barrot added.

Investigators say the attackers had used Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices located in Iran to carry out the attack, during which they gained internet access to the refrigeration systems and remotely cranked up temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight.

Millions of euros worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.

French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.

At least 300 of Intermarche’s stores and its Netto brand were affected. Cooperative U said more than 100 of its supermarkets were targeted, while Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected, and Monoprix reported that about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit.

Supermarkets in several other European countries reported similar refrigeration problems on November 2. Overnight temperature spikes were recorded in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. Dozens of stores and a food distribution hub were hit.

articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: In an awkward collision of symbolism and reality, US President Donald Trump celebrated Diwali's victory of good over
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: In an awkward collision of symbolism and reality, US President Donald Trump celebrated Diwali's victory of good over evil in the Oval Office last Friday just hours before a right-wing extremist he pardoned for January 6 violence disrupted an Indian community Diwali celebration in Seattle.Photos of the low-key Oval Office Diwali event came not from the White House but from those who attended the ceremony, including tech entrepreneur Vishal Gondal, who presented a Hanuman chalisa -- the devotional hymn to Lord Hanuman recited by millions for courage and strength -- to Trump on the occasion. It was another ironic outcome considering MAGA hardliners have also raged against a Hanuman statue in Sugarland, Texas.The Oval Office gathering included India's Ambassador to the US Vinay Kwatra, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, FBI Director Kash Patel, NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, Social Security Administration Deputy Commissioner Arjun Mody, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra and IBM CEO Arvind Krishna, and celebrity chef Vikas Khanna, among others. There was no media coverage of the event.The White House subsequently issued a presidential message in which Trump sent his “warmest greetings to Americans across our great Nation celebrating Diwali – the Festival of Lights.”“During this special time, families gather around flickering diyas, homes shine with the warmth of ancient traditions, and countless communities glow with the beauty of a celebration thousands of years in the making. This Diwali, we observe light’s enduring triumph over the forces of darkness and honor the goodness that lives within each and every one of us -- timeless values that have long enriched the great story of America,” the message read.It was a stirring sentiment, although the administration's record has provided plenty of material for those wondering about the darkness in question.Trump began his second presidency by pardoning or commuting the sentences of roughly 1,500 people charged or convicted in connection with January 6, including Jake Lang, who had faced serious charges over his participation in the Capitol assault. The sweeping clemency drew criticism from law-enforcement advocates, particularly given the violence inflicted on police officers that day.On Saturday, Lang and another activist interrupted performances at the Seattle Center Armory carrying signs reading "Deport All Dot Heads" and "Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians." The incident barely created a ripple in the administration, even though several lawmakers condemned the disruption and racist slogans.Despite the President’s gesture, an annual feature going back to the Bush White House, the Trump administration's hardline immigration policies and rhetoric targeting immigrants are widely seen to have contributed to an increasingly hostile political climate for immigrant communities. The Seattle episode offered a particularly ugly manifestation of that atmosphere, coming weeks after authorities thwarted a mass shooting plan targeting a Hindu temple in Illinois.Several lawmakers have condemned the Seattle incident, noting the rise in anti-India sentiment across the US “The racist, anti-Indian protests at a Diwali event in Seattle are despicable and must be unequivocally condemned. articles.title: France accelerates minimum wage hike in bid to quell protest
articles.summary: Unions slam the increase as insufficient, as the government seeks to defuse the unrest ahead of upcoming elections.
articles.body:
The French government has announced it will move a planned rise in the minimum wage forward by a month as it seeks to quell mass protests over the cost of living .

French ⁠Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced on Monday that the 1.6 percent increase in the minimum wage, originally planned for the start of 2027, will now take effect from December 1, 2026.

The move comes amid weeks of student-led demonstrations that started with calls for greater investment for the country’s underfunded schools but have morphed into broader protests and serious unrest – part of a wave across Europe.

The minimum monthly wage in France currently stands at 1,477.93 euros ($1,656); the increase raises it by 24 euros ($27) to 1,502 euros ($1,683).

“Regarding the SMIC [minimum wage], we have decided two things: to bring forward the increase to 1 December as opposed to 1 January, and to raise this increase to 1.6 per cent,” said Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou at a press conference.

This increase represents “the second-largest rise in 20 years; it should not be underestimated”, Lecornu told reporters, stressing that this boost is “not merely symbolic”.

“This increase has been carefully planned to ensure it does not lead to job losses,” the PM said.

The last rise came in June, when inflation levels triggered a 35-euro ($39) hike.

Despite the accelerated increases, the minimum wage still falls short of union demands. The CFDT, France’s largest union, has called for a 100-euro ($112) increase, while the left-wing CGT union is demanding a 10 percent rise, equivalent to around 150 euros ($168) a month.

CFDT head Marylise Leon said the increase was “insufficient”. ⁠CGT head Sophie Binet described it as “crumbs”.

The government is concerned about mounting social tensions five months before presidential elections.

Far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, who has been accused of encouraging the unrest, unveiled his programme on Saturday to some 17,000 supporters.

He pledged to boost the economy by capitalising on consumer spending and “through billions [of euros] that already exist”, adding that these savings “must be channelled towards our country’s environmental and social needs”.

articles.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people
articles.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.
articles.body:
At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.

The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.

Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan originally said the death toll was 16, but later Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died of their injuries, taking the toll to 17.

Eyewitnesses at the scene of the incident said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.

In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.

Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued.

At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.

The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.
